write.desc: Proof by induction on the natural numbers, in its ordinary, strong and well-ordering forms, together with the recursive definitions (sums, products, factorials, recurrences) that induction is used to reason about; these belong together because each recursive definition is the natural partner of an induction proof, and later parts use both constantly.

points.name: The principle of mathematical induction
points.what: Understand the principle: if P(1) holds and P(k) implies P(k+1) for every k, then P(n) holds for all natural numbers n. Be able to explain why the base case and the inductive step together reach every n, and why neither can be dropped.
outside: statements P(n) depending on a variable and the quantifier 'for all n'
what an implication 'if P then Q' claims

points.name: Writing an induction proof
points.what: Be able to write an induction proof in a clear standard layout: state P(n) explicitly, prove the base case, state the inductive hypothesis for an arbitrary k, and show exactly where it is used to reach P(k+1). Separate the scratch work of finding how P(k+1) follows from the final forward write-up.
outside: proof-writing conventions: stating assumptions and goal, scratch work versus final write-up

points.name: Sigma notation, products and factorials as recursive definitions
points.what: Read and use sigma and product notation and factorials, understood as recursive definitions (the sum to n+1 is the sum to n plus the next term; (n+1)! = (n+1) n!). Be able to split off the last term, shift an index and rewrite sums, which is the step most induction proofs about sums rely on.

points.name: Proving sum formulas by induction
points.what: Prove closed formulas for finite sums by induction, such as 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2, the sum of squares and the geometric sum, by splitting off the last term and using the inductive hypothesis. Understand that induction verifies a formula but does not by itself discover it.

points.name: Proving divisibility statements by induction
points.what: Prove statements such as '3 divides n^3 - n' or '6 divides 7^n - 1' for all n by induction, rewriting the (k+1) case so that the inductive hypothesis appears as a visible piece.
outside: definition of 'a divides b' for integers

points.name: Induction from any starting value
points.what: Prove statements that hold only for n at least some n0, such as 2^n > n^2 for n >= 5, by starting the base case at n0 and taking k >= n0 in the inductive step. Know how to check where a statement first becomes true and why the step may need k >= n0.

points.name: Proving inequalities by induction: Bernoulli's inequality
points.what: Prove inequalities by induction, where the inductive step uses the hypothesis plus one extra estimate, with Bernoulli's inequality (1 + x)^n >= 1 + nx for x >= -1 and integer n >= 1 as the key example. Know that this inequality is used later to bound powers and prove limits.

points.name: Sequences defined by a recurrence
points.what: Understand sequences defined recursively, by one or more starting values and a rule giving a(n+1) from earlier terms (for example a(n+1) = sqrt(2 + a(n)) or the Fibonacci numbers), and why induction guarantees such a definition determines every term. Be able to compute terms and guess patterns from them.

points.name: Proving properties of recursive sequences by induction
points.what: Prove by induction that a recursively defined sequence is bounded, positive, increasing or decreasing, or satisfies a closed formula, choosing the right statement P(n) (sometimes a stronger one than the claim) so that the inductive step goes through. These are exactly the facts later used to show such sequences converge.

points.name: Strong induction and when to use it
points.what: Use strong (complete) induction, where the inductive step assumes P(1), ..., P(k) rather than only P(k), and recognise when it is needed: when P(k+1) depends on cases further back, as in two-term recurrences like Fibonacci or the proof that every integer n >= 2 is a product of primes. Know how many base cases a given step requires.

points.name: The well-ordering principle
points.what: Understand that every nonempty set of natural numbers has a least element, that this is equivalent to induction, and use it to write proofs by minimal counterexample (assume the statement fails, take the smallest n where it fails, and derive a contradiction).

points.name: Common mistakes in induction proofs
points.what: Spot and avoid the typical errors: a missing or wrong base case, assuming P(n) for all n instead of for one k, an inductive step that silently fails for small k (as in the 'all horses are the same colour' argument), and too few base cases for strong induction.
